Predicting aircraft engine
remaining useful life

CMPS 261 · Final report · Group 16 · American University of Beirut
Moustapha Haydoura · Wassim Fawaz · Mohamad Khalil
20 November 2026

We estimate remaining useful life (RUL) from the NASA C-MAPSS FD001 simulated engine trajectories and ask whether sequence learning improves on classical models given comparable history. A 60/20/20 engine split separates fitting, model selection, and interval calibration. We compare linear regression, random forests, XGBoost, a one-dimensional CNN, and an LSTM, with controlled historical-feature ablations. The model selected by validation, CNN MSE, achieves 14.93 cycles RMSE and 11.51 cycles MAE on 100 official test endpoints. The strongest observed classical and neural test results are 13.51 (RF history) and 14.93 (CNN MSE) cycles, respectively. Nominal 90% intervals for the selected model cover 81% of test targets. We report tuning, split sensitivity, inference cost, and failure modes rather than treating one aggregate score as evidence of operational reliability.

RUL is the number of operating cycles left before an engine reaches the end of its simulated trajectory. Predicting this quantity could help prioritize maintenance, but a useful predictor must distinguish normal variation from degradation and expose uncertainty when that distinction is weak. FD001 provides a manageable setting for studying those questions; it does not represent actual in-flight failures [1,2].

Our research question has two parts: does including recent sensor history improve prediction, and does learning a sequence representation add value beyond engineered summaries of that same history? The second part is essential. Comparing a CNN with a current-reading baseline alone would confound model architecture with access to information.

For an engine ending at cycle T, the raw target at cycle t is T - t. The fitted target is min(T - t,125). This piecewise target reflects a modeling assumption that early healthy operation offers limited information about the eventual failure time; the cap is fixed from the existing project rather than tuned on test results. The primary evaluation still uses raw RUL. A second, explicitly labeled capped RMSE shows how much the evaluation changes when that assumption is also imposed on the target.

The retained channels are operating settings 1 and 2 and sensors 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 20, and 21: 14 sensors plus two settings, not 16 sensors. The original exclusion list is retained for FD001. Sensor 6 is near-constant; the other excluded channels are constant or effectively constant in this subset. The full variability audit is supplied in feature_audit.csv. Removing these channels does not establish that the remaining predictors are independent.

Min-max scaling is fitted only on the 60 fitting engines. Validation, calibration, and test observations use those same extrema, without refitting or clipping scaled inputs. Thirty-cycle windows remain within engine boundaries. The training label belongs to the final cycle of each window. All classical and neural models use the same endpoints, avoiding an advantage from extra training examples. The engine ID and absolute cycle index are excluded from predictors.

The shortest official test history has 31 cycles. The inference implementation nevertheless supports shorter histories by repeating the first observation on the left. No engine is silently dropped, and test targets are aligned by ID. There are 11 test labels above 125; the target cap alone imposes an RMSE floor of 3.74 cycles for predictions restricted to [0,125].

The mean capped training target is a no-information baseline. Ordinary least-squares linear regression provides an interpretable reference. Random forests average randomized regression trees [4]. XGBoost builds regularized boosted trees [3]. For each historical representation, all features are computed causally from the same 30-cycle window: current readings (16 values), current + mean + population standard deviation (48), and current + mean + standard deviation + least-squares slope per cycle (64).

The CNN follows the existing notebook: Conv1d(16,w,3) → ReLU → Conv1d(w,2w,3) → ReLU → MaxPool(2) → flatten → dense(64) → ReLU → scalar. Padding preserves temporal length. The LSTM uses one recurrent layer of width w, the last hidden output, and a 32-unit ReLU head [5]. Both consume the ordered 30 × 16 input. Convolution is a reasonable local temporal model [6], while the LSTM tests the originally proposed recurrent alternative. Neither architecture is assumed to outperform a tuned tree model.

The proposal specified linear regression, random forest, and LSTM; the progress report substituted XGBoost and CNN. The final experiment retains both sets. Boosting provides a regularized nonlinear baseline for the engineered summaries, while convolution tests whether short local patterns can be learned with parallel temporal filters. Restoring the proposal models makes these changes comparative choices rather than unsupported replacements. The exponential-loss instability mentioned in the progress report is not reproduced here; the weighted MSE is evaluated directly as a bounded-cost surrogate.

XGBoost uses histogram trees, row and column subsampling .8, and L2 regularization 5. Sensor-only and top-six ablations reuse the selected history-model configuration; they are not independently retuned. Neural targets are divided by 125. Adam uses weight decay 1e-5, batches of 256, gradient-norm clipping at 5, at most 35 epochs, and patience 8. The best checkpoint is restored. These small searches are documented experiments, not claims of exhaustive optimization.

With seed 42, 60 engines fit the models, 20 provide validation, and 20 remain reserved for calibration. For each validation engine, three distinct observed prefixes are drawn uniformly from endpoints allowing 30 observations and at most 150 remaining cycles. This produces 60 validation endpoints with equal engine representation. Candidate RMSE is computed against raw RUL. The asymmetric CNN deliberately selects by validation PHM instead; the final deployment candidate across model variants is still selected by validation raw RMSE. The prefix scheme approximates partial histories but is not guaranteed to match the official censoring distribution.

For d = predicted RUL - true RUL, RMSE = sqrt(mean(d²)) and MAE = mean(|d|). The PHM sum is Σ[exp(-d/13)-1] for d < 0 and Σ[exp(d/10)-1] for d ≥ 0 [2]. Positive errors therefore receive the larger penalty. The supplied notebook had these denominators reversed. Training the asymmetric CNN instead uses the stable surrogate mean[d² × (r if d > 0 else 1)], with r = 2 or 5, not the exponential score itself. All point predictions are clipped to [0,125].

5.4 Failure analysis and a tested mitigation

Figure 6. Endpoint predictions for historical XGBoost and both CNN objectives. Red points overestimate remaining life; blue points underestimate it. The horizontal dotted line is the fixed prediction cap.
Figure 7. Error magnitude and bias by true remaining-life range. Positive bias corresponds to overestimation. Stage metrics use disjoint groups of the same official test engines.

The asymmetric CNN reduced the overall frequency of overestimation from 58% to 51%. For the 25 engines with 30 or fewer cycles left, that frequency fell from 72% to 48%. Total PHM rose from 356.8 to 363.4 and raw RMSE from 14.93 to 15.15 cycles, so fewer optimistic estimates did not translate to a lower aggregate penalty. The two CNN variants also differ in selected architecture and checkpoint, limiting what we can attribute to the loss alone.

The cap necessarily underestimates targets above 125. Even below that threshold, similar sensor states can correspond to different remaining horizons because trajectories begin with different health states and degradation rates. The plots and subgroup errors are consistent with that ambiguity but do not identify its physical cause. A practical next experiment would compare uncapped or multi-stage targets using development engines only, followed by evaluation on an additional untouched subset.

5.5 Can the uncertainty estimates be trusted?

A separate set of 20 calibration engines supplies one randomly truncated endpoint each. For a fixed model, we calculate the absolute raw-RUL residual on each endpoint. The nominal 90% split-conformal radius is the 19th smallest of 20 residuals: ceil((20+1) × .9) = 19. Intervals are [max(0,prediction-q), prediction+q]. We do not cap the upper bound at 125, because the target is raw remaining life [7].

For CNN MSE, the radius is 21.97 cycles. On the official test engines, coverage is 81% and mean width is 42.87 cycles. These two quantities must be read together: a wide interval can cover many outcomes without providing a precise maintenance decision. Figure 8 checks whether aggregate coverage hides weaker performance in a particular life stage.

Figure 8. Nominal 90% residual intervals for the validation-selected model, sorted by true test RUL for visualization only. Right: empirical coverage by life stage; no test labels are used to set interval widths.
Table 3. Interval widths are in cycles. Calibration residuals are independent of fitting and model selection, but only 20 independent engines determine each radius.

Split conformal prediction relies on exchangeability between calibration and deployment examples. Our synthetic prefix selection and the official test censoring process may differ, so nominal 90% coverage is not an unconditional guarantee here. It is also a marginal statement, not a promise for every engine or life stage. We therefore report observed coverage and widths, avoid describing the intervals as validated safety bounds, and recommend additional independent calibration under the intended censoring process.

Historical features gave the clearest accuracy gain. XGBoost improved from 18.01 cycles test RMSE with current readings to 13.72 with historical summaries. The validation-selected CNN MSE reached 14.93, while RF history had the lowest observed test RMSE at 13.51. The paired 95% bootstrap interval for historical XGBoost minus CNN MSE spans [-2.45, 0.05] cycles, leaving the test advantage uncertain.

The overall results give limited reason to pay the CNN’s fitting cost on FD001. Historical XGBoost minus CNN validation RMSE ranged from -0.26 to +2.41 cycles across the three splits. The selected CNN fit took 5.9 times as long as the XGBoost fit, while both predicted a prepared batch of 100 histories in under 2 ms. For the 25 engines with 0–30 cycles remaining, the CNN reached 4.06 cycles RMSE, compared with 5.54 for historical XGBoost. A future study focused on near-failure decisions could validate directly on that horizon.

The principal methodological improvement is a comparison that controls information access and avoids test-driven tuning in this revision. The earlier RMSE 65.02 baseline and CNN RMSE 17.05 are not used as final evidence: no saved split, tuning history, checkpoint, or prediction file supports their reproduction, and the supplied scoring function reversed the PHM penalties. The new experiment reports both successful and unsuccessful variants, along with their resource costs and uncertainty.

The scope remains one simulated operating condition and fault mode. The 125-cycle cap creates a known long-horizon bias; calibration uses only 20 engines; repeated-split results are not independent CV; and the public test set had already been inspected in the progress report. Freezing the revised protocol cannot undo that historical exposure. Further work should use an untouched evaluation set, test uncapped or stage-specific targets, repeat training seeds within each split, and assess FD002-FD004 before making broader generalization claims.
